Neonates of the Broad stingray (Bathytoshia lata) are born with a disc width of 40 centimeters [Lb = 40 centimeters], a size that facilitates their survival in coastal nursery grounds. This initial dimension is notably modest when compared to the ultimate disc width of 260 centimeters [Li = 260 centimeters] that the species can achieve, a trajectory that reflects decades of sustained somatic growth. The gestation period, observed under controlled aquarium conditions, lasts 657 days at a stable temperature of 20.2 °C [T = 20.2 °C], yielding an age at birth of 657 days [ab = 657 days]. Such an extended gestation is characteristic of large, viviparous elasmobranchs and imposes a substantial maternal investment per pup, as the developing embryos rely entirely on yolk reserves during the lengthy incubation.

Sexual maturation in this species exhibits marked sexual dimorphism in size. Females first attain reproductive maturity at a disc width of 104.9 centimeters [Lp = 104.9 centimeters], while males reach puberty at the considerably smaller disc width of 74.9 centimeters [Lp = 74.9 centimeters]. This divergence is common among myliobatiform rays and is thought to reflect differences in the energetic demands of reproduction between the sexes. The larger size threshold for females likely correlates with the physical capacity required for successful gestation and parturition of relatively large pups. Field surveys conducted in the coastal waters of the southeastern Atlantic indicate that these size-based maturation schedules are consistent across the species’ geographic range.

The maximum lifespan documented for the Broad stingray is 10,220 days [am = 10,220 days], a longevity estimate derived from mark-recapture studies performed in waters with a mean temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This extraordinary longevity, exceeding twenty-eight years in the wild, positions Bathytoshia lata among the longest-lived batoids. Individuals require many years to complete their somatic growth before shifting energy toward reproduction, a life-history strategy that buffers against variable juvenile survival. The slow pace of life is further underscored by a low maximum reproductive rate, which is shaped by the warm-temperate thermal regime in which the ray resides.

Reproductive output is limited, with gravid females yielding a litter of six pups [N_R_i = a litter of six pups] approximately once every two years [F_R_i = approximately once every two years] in the thermal conditions typical of their subtropical habitat at 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This slow reproductive schedule, with a maximum of one litter every two years, is consistent with the species’ K-selected strategy and its occupation of a relatively stable, low-mortality environment. The combination of a modest litter size and an extended inter-birth interval means that population replenishment is gradual, rendering the species particularly vulnerable to overexploitation by directed fisheries.

Comparative analyses with other large dasyatids reveal that the Broad stingray’s disc width at birth of 40 centimeters [Lb = 40 centimeters] is intermediate between that of congeneric species from tropical and temperate regions. The ultimate disc width of 260 centimeters [Li = 260 centimeters] positions Bathytoshia lata as one of the largest stingrays in its family, a size that confers both competitive dominance and a reduced risk of predation. The age at birth of 657 days [ab = 657 days] at 20.2 °C [T = 20.2 °C] is unusually prolonged, even among viviparous chondrichthyans, and suggests that thermal conditions during gestation play a critical role in determining developmental rates. These life-history traits collectively define a slow, low-fecundity life cycle that requires careful conservation management.
